summary: Describes how Message Disposition Notifications, the read receipts defined in RFC 2298, should be handled when several mail clients share an IMAP mailbox. It addresses how clients decide who sends a receipt, and records that one was sent.

eli5.summary: When an email asks for a read receipt and you use several mail programs, they should not each send one. This note sets the rules to avoid duplicates.

questions: how do imap clients avoid duplicate read receipts
what is a message disposition notification in imap
subtitle: How several mail programs sharing one IMAP mailbox avoid sending the same read receipt twice.

tldr.problem: A message can ask for a read receipt, but when the same IMAP mailbox is reached from different places or different mail programs, each one might send its own receipt, because a single program only tracks sent receipts locally.
tldr.mechanism: Clients mark a message with the $MDNSent keyword on the server once a receipt has been sent or declined, and every client treats that keyword as meaning that no receipt may be sent.
tldr.outcome: No new IMAP command or response is needed, only a shared convention that clients follow and that servers must be able to store.

today: RFC 3503 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3501 and RFC 2298.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
RFC 3503 builds on the Message Disposition Notification (MDN) facility from RFC 2298. An MDN is the acknowledgement a recipient's mail program sends back when a message asks for one. RFC 2298 does not say how several mail user agents (MUAs) should cooperate when they use the Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP4) to reach one mailstore.

With a single MUA on a single computer, nothing special is needed. The MUA keeps track of the notifications it has sent in a local configuration. That breaks down when IMAP is used to reach the same mailstore from different locations or with different MUAs, because each one would have its own idea of what has been sent.
sections.eli5: If you check the same mailbox on your phone and your laptop, each one might tell the sender you read the letter. That is annoying, so they need a way to tell each other.

sections.title: The $MDNSent Keyword
sections.content:
The memo defines one new mailbox keyword, $MDNSent, which lets multiple MUAs know whether a requested receipt has been dealt with. It adds no new IMAP command or response. It describes a technique that MUAs should use to interoperate, and MUAs must use the keyword.

When a client opens a mailbox for the first time, it checks the PERMANENTFLAGS response code to see whether the server can store the keyword. To support MDN in IMAP, a server MUST support either $MDNSent itself or arbitrary message keywords.
sections.eli5: The keyword is a sticker on the letter that says 'receipt already handled'. Any mail program that sees the sticker leaves the letter alone.

sections.title: Client Behavior
sections.content:
The RFC modifies the timeline in Section 4 of RFC 2298. After the message is delivered, the MUA logs into the IMAP server, opens the mailbox and checks that it can store $MDNSent. It then generates automatic MDNs for messages that have neither the keyword nor the \Draft flag, and sets $MDNSent on every message that required an automatic MDN, whether or not the MDN was actually sent.

When the user acts on a message, the MUA performs the action and, with the user's permission, sends the proper MDN. If the MDN is saved to a mailbox with APPEND, the client MUST specify $MDNSent in that command. The MUA then sets the keyword on every message for which the user confirmed sending a disposition, or was explicitly prevented from doing so.

  • A client MUST NOT try to set the keyword if the server cannot store it permanently.
  • A client MUST be prepared for a NO reply to STORE, since a server may limit how many keywords a mailbox can hold, and SHOULD NOT send an MDN if it fails to store the keyword.
  • Once set, the keyword MUST NOT be unset by a client. A client MAY set it when the user declines to send a notification, which stops all other MUAs from sending one.
sections.eli5: Your mail program puts the sticker on as soon as it handles the receipt, even if you said no. Nobody is allowed to peel the sticker off later.

sections.title: Rules for Receiving, Copying, Sending and Drafts
sections.content:
A client MUST NOT send an MDN for a message that has the $MDNSent keyword or the \Draft flag, because some clients use \Draft to mark an incomplete message. If the keyword is present, the client MUST ignore all other flags and keywords when deciding whether to send an MDN.

The RFC rules out other flags as signals. A client MUST NOT use \Recent, because with several connections on one mailbox it is undefined which connection sees a message as recent. It MUST NOT use standard flags such as \Draft or \Answered to mean that an MDN was sent. It MAY use \Seen as one hint that an MDN must not be sent.

Copying and saving also matter. A client SHOULD verify that the keyword is preserved on a COPY, and MUST set it correctly when it copies a message between servers with APPEND. When saving a sent message or an unfinished message to any folder, the client MUST set the keyword so that another client does not send an MDN for it.
sections.eli5: Your own sent letters and half-written drafts get the sticker right away so nobody sends a receipt for them. A program must also not guess from other clues like the 'new' mark.

sections.title: Server Behavior
sections.content:
A server follows this memo if it meets either Section 4.1 or Section 4.2. A server that supports arbitrary keywords needs no changes. A server that supports only $MDNSent MUST preserve it on COPY, and is expected to support SEARCH KEYWORD $MDNSent if it supports SEARCH by flag.

If the server also supports the IMAP ACL extension (RFC 2086), it SHOULD preserve the keyword on COPY even when the client lacks the w right. This prevents a duplicate MDN. The server MUST still check that the client may perform the copy under the ACL rules.
sections.eli5: The mailbox server just has to remember the sticker, even when letters are copied to another folder. Then the sticker travels with the letter.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows a client opening INBOX. A server that stores arbitrary keywords lists \* in its PERMANENTFLAGS, while a server that stores only the one keyword lists $MDNSent. A successful STORE 4 +FLAGS ($MDNSent) returns a FETCH showing the flag, and a failed one returns NO.

One example stresses that clients and servers MUST treat the keyword as case insensitive: after a fetch showing $MdnSENt and $MdnSENT on some messages, a SEARCH KEYWORDS $mdnsent returns messages 2, 4 and 5.
sections.eli5: It does not matter if you write the sticker's name in big or small letters. They all mean the same sticker.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that there are no known security issues with this extension beyond those already found in RFC 2298 or IMAP4. The one point it flags is that Section 4.3 changes the ACL checking requirements for a server that implements the ACL extension.
sections.eli5: The sticker adds no new danger. The only special thing is a small rule about who may copy a letter.

data.title: Setting the keyword
data.code:
C: a200 STORE 4 +FLAGS ($MDNSent)
S: * 4 FETCH (FLAGS (\Flagged \Seen $MDNSent))
S: a200 OK STORE completed

C: a200 STORE 4 +FLAGS ($MDNSent)
S: a200 NO STORE failed : no space left to store $MDNSent keyword
